{{short description|Iranian-born British nuclear physicist and filmmaker}}
{{unreliable sources|date=January 2020}}

[[File:Taghi_Amirani_in_2020.png|thumb|right|alt=Taghi Amirani physics|Taghi Amirani 2020]]
'''Taghi Amirani''' is an [[Iran]]ian-born English [[physicist]] and [[documentarian|documentary filmmaker]] who lives in the [[United Kingdom]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Kenigsberg |first=Ben |date=2020-08-19 |title='Coup 53' Review: International Underhandedness, Still Mysterious |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/08/19/movies/coup-53-review.html |access-date=2022-09-19 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> He has worked primarily in television, prior to the release of the film documentary ''[[Coup 53]]'' in 2019.<ref name=":0" />

==Early life and education==
Taghi Amirani grew up in [[Iran]].<ref name="auto1">{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wuA0oR9p8xM |title=10,000 Questions, One Certainty: Taghi Amirani at TEDxDanubia 2014 |date=June 2014 |type=Online video |publisher=[[TEDx Talks]] |place=Budapest, Hungary |via=YouTube}}</ref>

In 1975 he moved to [[England]] to attend school. He went on to study physics at the [[University of Nottingham]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Durrani |first=Matin |date=2022-08-12 |title=Ask me anything: Taghi Amirani – a physicist turned documentary-film maker |url=https://physicsworld.com/ask-me-anything-taghi-amirani-a-physicist-turned-documentary-film-maker/ |access-date=2022-09-19 |website=Physics World |language=en-GB}}</ref> His final year project at University of Nottingham was ''Shades of Black'', a documentary about the experience of entering a [[black hole]].

He took a postgraduate film and television course at the [[University of Bristol]], where he made ''Mechanics of Love'', a black-and-white silent comedy film.<ref name="auto">[https://wearemany.com/the-film/castcrew/taghi-amirani/ Taghi Amirani; We Are Many];</ref>

== Career ==
=== Early television work ===
His first job after leaving the University of Bristol was at [[Thames TV]], where he worked as a researcher on documentaries. In 1989 he made his debut as a producer and director with an episode of Channel 4's ''Equinox'' series entitled "Earth Calling Basingstoke". He went on to make several dozen 36 full-length films, in addition to a number of short films and commercials.

In addition to ''Equinox'', he has written, directed, and/or produced episodes of the series ''True Stories'', ''He Play'', ''Q.E.D.'', ''Short Stories'', ''Auction'', ''The Jupiter Collision'', ''Holy Places'', ''Encounters'', ''Picture This'', ''Edinburgh or Bust'', ''Correspondent'', ''War on Iraq'', ''This Time Next Year'', and ''Wide Angle''. He also made the six-part series ''Mad about Machines'', about the relationship between people and their machines. {{Citation needed|date=August 2020}} He was field producer and cinematographer for the 2003 TV documentary ''Inside Mecca'', a [[National Geographic]] production that followed three pilgrims to [[Mecca]] from different parts of the world.

=== ''The Dispossessed'' ===
After the [[United States invasion of Afghanistan|U.S.]] began its invasion of [[Afghanistan]] in November 2001, Amirani went to that country and interviewed ordinary Afghans at a [[Taliban]]-run refugee camp. The result was ''The Dispossessed'', which was aired in January 2002 as an episode of the [[BBC]] series ''Correspondent''. When criticized for showing some scenes of suffering, he said in his defense that “we have a choice of switching off to other people's suffering and getting on with our lives or getting involved and seeing what our governments are doing in our name. It is our job to convey that information – to bring the suffering of these people who are caught between many evils. They were oppressed by the Taliban, before that they were invaded by the [[Russia]]ns, they've gone through years of war and now they are being bombed by the Americans.”<ref name="auto1"/><ref name="auto2">{{Cite web |last=O’Hanlon |first=Alice |date=December 5, 2005 |title=Taghi Amirani - Red Lines & Deadlines |url=https://www.englishpen.org/posts/events/taghi-amirani-red-lines-deadlines/ |access-date=2022-09-19 |website=English Pen |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Freeman |first=Robert |date=18 January 2002 |title=Ask Taghi Amirani |language=en-GB |work=BBC |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/programmes/correspondent/1766320.stm |access-date=2022-09-19}}</ref>

=== ''Red Lines and Deadlines'' ===
Amirani has explained that since he was not in Iran during the [[1979 revolution]], he “always felt I had missed the first-hand experience of an important chapter in my country’s history. Instead, from my adopted home in England, I watched the revolution and the ensuing 26 years unfold on TV.” Over the years he came to feel that “what I was watching were developments in my homeland interpreted through the prism of mainly Western journalists and filmmakers. It was time to stop watching the stream of stereotype and customary clichés from the outside, and go find out for myself.” In 2004 he went to Iran “to look for stories” and saw a copy of ''Shargh'', a reformist newspaper.<ref>Red Lines and Deadlines - Filmmaker Notes: Director Taghi Amirani; PBS; [https://www.pbs.org/wnet/wideangle/uncategorized/red-lines-and-deadlines-filmmaker-notes-director-taghi-amirani/2533/]</ref> He ended up writing, producing, directing, and photographing a 2004 documentary, ''Red Lines and Deadlines'', about the staff of the newspaper and its reformist politics. It was first aired on [[PBS]] as part of the series ''Wide Angle''. The ''[[Wall Street Journal]]'' described the film as “an unprecedented look into the [[Orwellian]] world of Iranian journalism.”<ref name="auto2"/>

=== ''Coup 53'' ===
He wrote, produced, directed, and photographed the documentary ''[[Coup 53]]'', which was released in 2019.<ref name=":0" /> The film recounts [[Operation Ajax]], the 1953 coup in Iran engineered by the [[CIA]] and [[MI6]] to overthrow the Prime Minister [[Mohammad Mosaddegh|Mohammad Mossadegh]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=McCarthy |first=Todd |date=2020-07-31 |title=Todd McCarthy: 'Coup 53' And A Great Documentary's Struggle To Find Its Audience |url=https://deadline.com/2020/07/coup-53-documentary-taghi-amirani-iran-todd-mccarthy-1202999556/ |access-date=2022-09-19 |website=Deadline |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Thorpe |first=Vanessa |date=2020-11-01 |title=Release of lauded Iranian documentary halted amid dispute with TV film-makers |url=http://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/nov/01/release-of-lauded-iranian-documentary-halted-amid-dispute-with-tv-film-makers |access-date=2022-09-19 |website=the Guardian |language=en}}</ref> He visited the [[National Security Archive]] at [[George Washington University]] in order to make a portion of the film.<ref name=":0" /> This film was co-produced by Ahmad Kiarostami and co-written and edited by [[Walter Murch]].<ref name=":1" />

=== Other professional activities ===
Taghi Amirani has served as a jury member at the International [[Emmys]], [[Royal Television Society]], [[One World Media Awards]], and [[Sheffield International Documentary Festival]].  He was awarded a [[TED Fellowship]] in 2009, and the next year received a TED Senior Fellowship in 2010.  In a 2014 [[TEDx]] Talk he spoke about the importance of “embracing uncertainty.”<ref name="auto1"/><ref name="auto"/>

== Personal life ==
Amirani lives in London. He ran the [[New York Marathon]] in 2006 and 2010.<ref name="auto"/>
